newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran artists optimistic Khatami will bring change.
newsitem.headline: Iran artists optimistic Khatami will bring change.

text.p: Artists toured Tehran cinemas on Monday showering crowds with flowers, sweets and posters of new President Mohammad Khatami -- the man they hope will make the Islamic Republic of Iran more tolerant.
"Mr Khatami is very good for artists," said Malake Rangbar, an actress who long predates Iran's 1979 Islamic revolution. "He will make change in the country."
Hundreds gathered to join in the celebrations at cinemas after Khatami, 54, took the oath of office on Monday.
"He was culture minister and we know him. He will make many changes and we hope things will be better than before," said actor Ramezany Far.
Current restrictions on the arts range from a ban on satellites and films showing a mother kissing her son to songs by popular Iranian artists living abroad.
"I have new tapes, I have new videos," a black marketeer whispered to a reporter shortly before crowds gathered in a busy Tehran shopping street.
A 25-year-old applied chemistry student in the crowd was less optimistic than the artists.
Khatami "will make only little change but even if he wants to make (drastic social changes) he cannot," said Shereen, who was covered from head to toe in line with Iran's strict dress code for women.
But she wore sunglasses and makeup -- considered provocative by some of the country's conservatives.

Analysts and diplomats say Khatami, seen as a moderate, middle-level Moslem Shi'ite clergyman among Iran's ruling mullahs, could face tough resistance from the conservative-dominated parliament if he embarked on a programme of change.

In 1992, Khatami was forced to resign as culture minister by conservatives who accused him of failing to strike strongly against what they saw as a Western cultural invasion and for allowing films, plays and books which they said clashed with Islam.

Later satellite dishes, a major window for Iranians to the outside world, were banned by parliament and confiscated. Diplomats said Khatami in pre-election television debates turned down several invitations to back the move, but he also did not commit himself to bringing back satellites if he won.
Many artists, youths and women, who gave Khatami an overwhelming victory in May's election, expect the new president to relax some social constraints.
"The scarf is enough, why this?" one women at the cinema asked, pointing at the traditional chador -- a black cloak worn in public by many women in Iran.
At home, many Tehran women receive male guests, including foreigners, in Western clothes.
Iran News daily said on Monday: "If we ask the people around us about their expectations from President Khatami, they will immediately respond by wishing for social justice...

"And the right to spend their free time enjoying reasonable and proper entertainment without obstruction by unauthorised persons" -- an apparent reference to members of the militant Ansar-e Hizbollah (Supporters of the Party of God) who have in the past attacked people on the streets for what they considered immoral dress or behaviour.
A mullah, who passed by a cinema on his way home, calmly commented on the celebrations by saying he did not expect Khatami to shake the country up.
"No," he said. "We all obey Islam and Khatami is a clergyman who is committed to Islam."
